profiles.meeting_scenario: St. Anselm Health System's legal department is holding a planning meeting to organize the legal and regulatory review of a manuscript that the clinical quality team wants to submit to a healthcare journal. The manuscript describes a medication-reconciliation improvement project across the main hospital and one community affiliate and has been drafted using the SQUIRE guidelines and their explanation-and-elaboration framework. Because the paper includes unit-level outcome tables, EHR workflow screenshots, and discussion of a project that began as local quality improvement and later expanded systemwide, the legal team needs to plan what review steps are required before submission. The agenda is to decide what materials must be collected, how the legal review will be sequenced, who will handle privacy and institutional-clearance tasks, and what timeline will support the authors' target submission in early June. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for obtaining the necessary records, completing legal review, and telling the authors when the manuscript is ready to move forward.

members.name: Elena Park
members.role: Senior Counsel, Academic Affairs and Publications
members.expertise: Publication clearance, institutional authorship policies, research and academic-affiliation issues for an academic medical center
members.background: Elena is an in-house attorney who supports physician-authors and hospital leadership on publications, conference abstracts, and collaboration agreements; before joining the legal department, she worked closely with a medical school's research administration office.
members.private_state: Elena wants to keep the clinician-authors on schedule and avoid becoming the reason the manuscript misses the journal window; she prefers to start legal review early, even if the paper is still being polished, and is mainly concerned with preventing obvious institutional or contractual problems.
hidden_assumptions: A 'final draft' is the version that is stable enough for legal review, even if co-authors will still make stylistic edits afterward.
The existing quality-improvement determination letter in the file is probably the relevant one unless the manuscript explicitly reframes the project as research.
A manuscript is 'cleared for submission' once legal sees no blocking issue, even if other administrative sign-offs are still processed afterward.
A legal de-identification review normally focuses on the main manuscript and embedded figures/tables; supplements and journal-form attachments are usually handled later unless someone flags them.

members.name: David Morales
members.role: Associate General Counsel, Privacy and Regulatory Compliance
members.expertise: HIPAA, state privacy law, peer-review protections, quality-improvement oversight, and regulatory risk in healthcare publications
members.background: David is an in-house healthcare lawyer who previously served in a hospital privacy office and now advises on disclosures in publications, presentations, and external sharing of operational data.
members.private_state: David wants to prevent inadvertent disclosure of protected health information or privileged quality-review material; he is less worried about author convenience than about making sure the institution has a complete defensible record before anything leaves the organization.
hidden_assumptions: A 'final draft' means the near-submission version after all substantive author revisions are done, because privacy review should not be repeated on moving text.
The relevant determination letter would be the newer systemwide or rollout-stage determination if the paper reports results from more than the original pilot unit.
A de-identification pass includes appendices, acknowledgments, screenshots, embedded dates, site references, and any supplemental material going to the journal.
A manuscript is not truly 'cleared for submission' until the necessary institutional approvals are complete, including any required privacy or quality-oversight sign-off.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members refer to getting the 'final draft' before review begins.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the first version that is stable enough to start legal review, even if authors will still make polishing edits after counsel comments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: David means the near-submission version that authors do not expect to change materially after privacy and regulatory review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In publication planning, 'final draft' is a routine phrase that often functions as shorthand rather than a carefully defined milestone, so both lawyers hear a familiar term and assume the same practical meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which determination letter is already 'in the file'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members mention relying on 'the determination letter' for the project.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the 2023 internal determination issued when the medication-reconciliation work began on the pilot medical unit as a local quality-improvement activity.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: David is thinking of the later 2024 determination or oversight record that would cover the expanded multi-site rollout discussed in the manuscript's results.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know the project had prior institutional review activity, and each assumes there is one obvious controlling document; because neither expects multiple similarly named records to matter at this planning stage, the reference sounds unambiguous.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that David will do a 'de-identification pass' before submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes this review covers the main manuscript file, including the tables and figures inserted into it, while authors will handle supplementary appendix details and journal uploads unless a problem is raised.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: David assumes the de-identification pass covers everything going out externally for the submission package, including supplements, acknowledgments, appendix dates, screenshots, and any supporting files that could reveal patients, providers, or privileged committee structures.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a standard single task, and both participants are accustomed to saying it without enumerating file boundaries; because the meeting is about planning rather than line-by-line review, the hidden perimeter of the task remains invisible.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about telling the authors when the manuscript is 'cleared for submission.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means legal has no objection to the manuscript being sent on, with remaining institutional forms or courtesy notifications able to follow in parallel.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: David means all required institutional permissions and regulatory sign-offs have been completed, so the authors may actually transmit the paper to the journal immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is cooperative and outcome-oriented, so it feels like obvious agreement on the end state; the deeper question of what threshold satisfies 'cleared' is second-order administrative detail that neither expects needs unpacking in a short planning meeting.

turns.inner_thought: I want to get in early enough that legal is not the bottleneck. For this kind of manuscript, I do not need every comma settled before we start; if the draft is stable enough, I can catch affiliation, authorship, and institutional issues while the clinicians keep polishing. The goal is to keep them on their early-June target and avoid a last-minute scramble.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to use this slot to set the review plan for the medication-reconciliation manuscript. The quality team is writing it in the SQUIRE format, and they want to hit an early-June submission, so I'd like us to be clear on what we need, how we sequence the review, and who owns which pieces.

turns.inner_thought: For me, privacy review should happen on the near-submission package, not on a moving target. If they keep changing language, screenshots, dates, or examples after I review, we lose confidence in the record. And the de-identification pass needs to cover everything going out, not just the body text.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Once we have the final draft and the related materials, I can block time for the de-identification pass and give them a realistic turnaround. The sooner I can see the package that's actually heading out, the easier it is to keep this tight.

turns.inner_thought: I should be able to start next week if they send the version they've stabilized for legal eyes, even if they still tweak wording afterward. And I can save time by pulling the 2023 QI determination already in the file from when this started on the pilot unit; unless they have recast the paper as research, that should be the key document.
turns.utterance: I expect to get the final draft next week, or at least close enough for us to begin. On my side, I'll start by pulling the determination letter that's already in the file so we have the baseline paperwork in hand.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if the oversight record for the broader rollout is already there, that will help anchor the review. And if I can do a full de-identification pass across the submission package, we should be in good shape to say it's cleared for submission once the institutional pieces line up.
turns.utterance: If the determination letter is already there, that should definitely help. And after the de-identification pass, we should be getting pretty close to cleared for submission, assuming nothing unusual jumps out.

turns.inner_thought: To keep momentum, I should collect the main manuscript file with the tables and screenshots embedded, since that is usually enough for the first legal read. I don't want the appendix to hold up review if the authors are still assembling it or formatting it for the journal.
turns.utterance: To keep this moving, I can gather the manuscript itself with the embedded tables and screenshots, and I can let the corresponding author keep assembling any supplementary appendix in parallel. That way we're not waiting on every last attachment before we start.

turns.inner_thought: I need to be explicit enough that they send the whole package, but without turning this into a long lecture. My de-identification pass is not just the main file; acknowledgments can identify people or committees, dates can triangulate cases, site references can expose units, and appendices or screenshots often carry the biggest risk.
turns.utterance: That's fine as a workflow, just so long as for the de-identification pass I can also see the acknowledgments, site references, dates, and any appendix material that will accompany the journal submission. Those are often where the avoidable issues show up.

turns.inner_thought: Once legal is comfortable there is no blocking issue, I can tell the team to proceed and let research administration catch up on its side. I don't want the authors sitting idle while routine forms circulate.
turns.utterance: Understood. Then once the manuscript is cleared for submission, I'll alert research administration and let the authors move ahead with the journal forms so we don't lose time at the end.

turns.inner_thought: I want to make sure no one treats legal comfort as the same thing as completed institutional permission. Given that the paper discusses the expansion beyond the original pilot, the relevant oversight sign-off needs to match the broader stage of the project reflected in the manuscript, not just the earliest version in the file.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I'd just want the clearance to line up with whatever oversight sign-off corresponds to the determination letter, especially since the paper discusses the broader rollout. If those pieces track together, the submission position is much cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: This seems straightforward: I get the draft that's ready enough for legal review, pull the existing determination letter, and hand David what he needs for his review of the manuscript package. That should keep the team on schedule without overcomplicating the intake.
turns.utterance: Great. So the working split is: I'll collect the final draft and the determination letter, and then you'll handle the de-identification pass once the materials come in. If anything is obviously missing at intake, I'll circle back to the authors right away.

turns.inner_thought: If I receive the near-submission package with the oversight record and all outbound materials, I can usually turn this around within several business days. The biggest risk is incomplete files; if the package is complete, we should be able to reach actual institutional clearance without major drama.
turns.utterance: That works. From receipt of the final draft to clearance, I'd budget about three to five business days on my side if the file is complete. I don't expect major obstacles here, as long as what comes in is the full set of materials we need.
